%%
%% The abstract is a short summary of the work to be presented in the
%% article.
\begin{abstract}
The basic theory of threads and locks in separation logic is well understood. However, locks as they are actually implemented have further variations and subtleties, including restrictions on transferring locks between threads, recursive mutexes, and classes designed for RAII patterns. In this paper, we present separation logic specifications for the C++ mutex library in the BRiCk logic. We identify and abstract out common patterns, including a mechanism for tracking a thread's mutex ownership, which can be used to enforce the mutex library's requirements. We demonstrate that our specifications are satisfied by implementations that explicitly track and check the owning thread, and thus do not satisfy the standard separation logic specifications for locks. We also show in a case study that our tracking logic is modular, so that even though mutexes require thread-specific predicates, the fact that a class uses a mutex internally can be hidden from the class's clients. %qualify a little -- we do need my_mutexes
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Mechanized concurrent separation logic (CSL) has advanced to the stage where we can prove correctness of programs in real languages, using logics like VST~\cite{vst}, BRiCk~\cite{brick}, or RustBelt~\cite{rustbelt} that give Hoare rules for every operation in the language. However, specification of language features alone is not enough to verify real code: most languages ship with extensive standard libraries, and programmers treat these libraries as if they were language primitives. This makes standard libraries a high-value target for specification and verification: they usually have only one or a few implementations and are used in almost all other code in the language. In this paper, we focus on the concurrency support library of C++, which includes threads, atomic operations, mutexes/locks, and futures. Threads, atomics, and locks have been thoroughly studied in concurrent separation logic, but C++'s locks include some restrictions and variants that have not previously been formalized.

First, unlike the standard separation-logic treatment of locks, C++ mutex operations place restrictions on which threads can perform them and whether they are currently held. For instance, the basic \lstinline{std::mutex} class must be released by the same thread that acquired it, cannot be acquired twice by the same thread, and must not be held when deallocated. One might expect that acquiring a lock twice in one thread would lead to deadlock, but in fact violating any of these conditions is \emph{undefined behavior}, meaning that it could lead to unsafe behavior and must not occur in verified code. We develop a general mechanism for tracking a thread's lock ownership, based on a reusable ghost state pattern, and use it to enforce the standard library's restrictions.

Second, the standard library includes three main variants of mutexes\footnote{The library also includes timed variants of each mutex type, on which attempts to acquire may time out, but from the separation logic perspective these are identical to the non-timed variants.}: ordinary mutex, recursive mutex, and shared mutex (i.e., reader-writer lock). Recursive mutexes, which can be acquired multiple times by a single thread, have not previously been formalized in separation logic, but are widely used in object-oriented programming---they allow a thread-safe method to acquire a lock on its object's contents even if it may be called from within another thread-safe method. We give specifications for all three variants, including a specification of recursive mutexes that allows generic reasoning over whether the lock is already held.

Finally, the standard library includes a collection of mutex container classes following the Resource Acquisition Is Initialization (RAII) pattern, where a resource (in this case, a mutex) is acquired when the container is created and released when it is destroyed. These classes are generic in the underlying type of mutex, using C++'s \emph{named requirement} feature (similar to \emph{interfaces} in other OO languages); the underlying mutex need only meet the \lstinline{BasicLockable} named requirement, supporting the \lstinline{lock} and \lstinline{unlock} methods. We develop a separation logic interface corresponding to \lstinline{BasicLockable} that is satisfied by all three of our mutex variants, and use it as a parameter to our RAII class specifications. In keeping with the OO principle of encapsulation, when an object uses a mutex in a well-structured way (whether through RAII or manually), tracking predicates need not appear in the object's representation predicate, allowing it to be transferred freely between threads as in conventional CSL.

In summary, our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
\item Specifications of standard, recursive, and shared mutexes as described in the C++ standard library.
\item Implementations of each mutex type that follow the library standard and thus do not satisfy the usual SL lock specifications, but are proven to satisfy our specifications.
\item A ghost-state library for thread identity tracking that we use to build the basic ownership predicates of the mutex specifications.
\item A generic interface for mutexes, corresponding to the \lstinline{BasicLockable} named requirement, and specifications for C++'s lock management objects that are parameterized by this interface.
\item A case study showing that thread-tracking predicates can be encapsulated inside an object, so that ownership of the object itself can be transferred between threads in the standard manner.
\end{itemize}

\section{Background}
\subsection{Lock Specifications in Separation Logic}
There are two common styles of CSL lock specification: invariant-based, and logically atomic (sometimes called TaDA-style~\cite{dRP+:TaDA-ecoop14}). In the invariant style, a lock $\ell$ protects an invariant $P$ (represented as $\mathsf{is\_lock}(\ell, P)$), and acquire and release are specified as:
\begin{mathpar}
\{\ell \mapsto \mathsf{lock}(P)\}\ \texttt{lock}(\ell)\ \{\ell \mapsto \mathsf{lock}(P) \ast \mathsf{locked}(\ell) \ast P\}

\{\ell \mapsto \mathsf{lock}(P) \ast \mathsf{locked}(\ell) \ast P\}\ \texttt{unlock}(\ell)\ \{\ell \mapsto \mathsf{lock}(P)\}
\end{mathpar}
In the atomic style, a lock is simply in one of two states, represented by e.g. a boolean that is $\mathsf{true}$ when the lock is held. Then acquire and release can be specified as:
\begin{mathpar}
\fforall b.\ \langle \ell \mapsto b \rangle\ \texttt{lock}(\ell)\ \langle \neg b \ast \ell \mapsto \mathsf{true} \rangle

\langle \ell \mapsto \mathsf{true} \rangle\ \texttt{unlock}(\ell)\ \langle \ell \mapsto \mathsf{false} \rangle
\end{mathpar}
While one thread is trying to acquire the lock, its state is unknown and may shift back and forth due to the behavior of other threads; at the lock's linearization point, we observe that the lock is not held ($\neg b$), and shift it to the held state ($\mathsf{true}$). By combining these specifications with a global invariant of the form $P \vee \ell \mapsto \mathsf{true}$, we can derive the invariant-style specs: an acquiring thread trades its ownership of the lock $\ell \mapsto \mathsf{true}$ for the invariant $P$, and then returns it before releasing the lock. (Less obviously, the TaDA-style specs can also be derived from invariant-style specs, using an invariant that is simply a ghost variable indicating the state $b$ of the lock%; see \citet{} for more details
.)

These specifications capture the core idea of mutual exclusion: at most one thread holds the lock at any point in time, and so the protected resources can safely be accessed by that thread. They can also easily be shown to be satisfied by a simple implementation, such as a spinlock. Furthermore, they can be used to verify very flexible synchronization patterns, such as the following \emph{daring concurrency} pattern:
\[\begin{array}{l || l}
\texttt{acquire(a);} & \texttt{acquire(b);}\\
\texttt{*x = *x + 1;} & \texttt{*x = *x + 1;}\\
\texttt{release(b);} & \texttt{release(a);}
\end{array}\]
In this program, each thread passes ownership of its lock to the other via another lock: if the left thread executes first, then when the second thread acquires \texttt{b} it also gains permission to release \texttt{a} (in the form of $\mathsf{locked}(a)$), and vice versa. Indeed, the ability to verify daring synchronization was one of the original strengths of concurrent separation logic~\cite{csl}.

However, the locks used in systems programming languages are not generally implemented this way, instead building on operating system primitives (e.g., Linux's futex~\cite{futex}) and highly optimized libraries (e.g., Pthread~\cite{pthread}) whose behavior depends on the thread holding the lock. This leads to both additional restrictions---e.g., locks may only be released by the thread that acquired them, or can only be deallocated if not held---and additional features---e.g., locks may be recursive, so that the holder can re-acquire them any number of times and only exits the critical section after performing an equal number of releases. In this paper, we show how to extend the simple lock specs to account for the restrictions and features of the mutexes in C++'s standard library.

\subsection{The BRiCk Logic for C++}
\label{brick}

\newcommand{\currentthread}[1]{\ensuremath{\mathtt{tid}(#1)}}

BRiCk~\cite{brick} is an Iris-based program logic for C++, inspired by Iris's HeapLang and the Verified Software Toolchain's logic for C~\cite{vst}. Its predicates and rules are similar to those of standard Iris instances, with special support for object-oriented data and templates. %anything else of note?
Unlike most Iris instances, it does not carry an adequacy proof that connects its rules to an operational semantics (indeed, there is no complete operational semantics for C++); it is an axiomatic semantics in the traditional sense. Its rules are justified by comparison to the (proved-sound) rules of HeapLang and VST, and by compiling and running example programs and checking that their behavior matches their specifications. %TODO cite previous brick paper/projects as justification

One feature of BRiCk that is particularly relevant to our work is thread-specific predicates. In ordinary separation logic, all predicates can be transfered between threads: if thread $t_1$ owns $x \mapsto v$ and then synchronizes with $t_2$ via a lock or atomic operation, then afterwards $t_2$ may own $x \mapsto v$. This is problematic when the behavior of a function depends on the calling thread. BRiCk solves this using Iris's \emph{monotonic predicates}, previously used in weak-memory logics~\cite{igps} %and others
. Every BRiCk predicate is implicitly indexed by a thread ID, and a predicate $\currentthread{t}$ asserts that the current thread's ID is $t$. All other primitive predicates, such as memory ownership, are \emph{objective} and can be freely transferred between threads. This allows us to specify the fact that, e.g., a C++ \lstinline{mutex} can only be released by the thread that acquired it.

\section{RAII Lock Classes}

\newcommand{\ulock}[0]{\ensuremath{\mathsf{ulock}}}

Managing locks manually is error-prone: it is easy to introduce deadlock by acquiring the same lock twice, forgetting to release a lock, or having a set of locks that are not always acquired and released in the same order, and releasing a lock that has not been acquired is undefined behavior. The Resource Acquisition Is Initialization (RAII) pattern aims to avoid these problems by aligning ownership of a lock with the lifetime of an object: the lock is acquired when the object is created, and released when the object is destroyed, thus benefiting from the guarantees of the language's memory management (an object will only be created and destroyed once each, will only be destroyed after it is created, will eventually be destroyed if unused, etc.). The C++ standard library includes a set of RAII lock classes, which we specify here. Intuitively, their specifications are simple: the object's constructor has the same specification as the underlying lock's \lstinline{lock} method, and the destructor has the same specification as the underlying \lstinline{unlock}. %but: we are the first to specify RAII at all in SL? in practice their use is more complicated (because of optional acquiring, detaching, etc.)? showing that they can actually be used as desired is nontrivial?
%we verify the actual standard library implementations of these classes?!

\subsection{Generic \lstinline{lock} and \lstinline{unlock}}
\label{basic-lockable}
The \lstinline{BasicLockable} named requirement describes the common interface
of types that provide \lstinline{lock()} and \lstinline{unlock()}
operations~\cite{ISO:2024:IIP}.  An invocation of \lstinline{lock()} blocks
until the calling thread acquires the lock, and \lstinline{unlock()} releases a
lock owned by the calling thread.  The caller must not already own the lock
when invoking \lstinline{lock()}, and must own it when invoking
\lstinline{unlock()}.  This is a requirement on a type, rather than a concrete
C++ class: \lstinline{std::mutex}, \lstinline{std::recursive_mutex}, and
user-defined lock types can all implement it.  Generic classes such as
\lstinline{lock_guard} can therefore operate on any such implementation.

We represent an implementation of \lstinline{BasicLockable} by a predicate
$R(q,x)$ describing fractional ownership $q$ of a lock with abstract state
$x$, together with two predicates $L(m,x,K)$ and $U(m,x,K)$.  These predicates
give the resources required to lock and unlock the object at $m$ and describe
their result through the continuation $K$.  The generic specifications are:
\begin{mathpar}
  \spectriple
    {m\mapsto R(q,x)\ast L(m,x,K)}
    {\texttt{m.lock()}}
    {m\mapsto R(q,x)\ast K}

  \spectriple
    {m\mapsto R(q,x)\ast U(m,x,K)}
    {\texttt{m.unlock()}}
    {m\mapsto R(q,x)\ast K}
\end{mathpar}
The representation predicate is preserved by both operations, while the
implementation-specific predicates describe the change in logical ownership.
For example, the \lstinline{std::mutex} instance defines $L$ to exchange the
calling thread's $\mathsf{not\_locked}$ token for the protected resource and its
\texttt{locked} token; it defines $U$ to perform the reverse exchange.  The
recursive and shared mutexes instantiate the same interface with their own
ghost states.  Thus clients can use the two generic specifications without
depending on the particular mutex representation.

\subsection{\lstinline{lock_guard}}
\begin{figure}[htb]
\begin{lstlisting}
  std::mutex mutex_;
  int size;

  bool get_size() {
    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mutex_);
    return size;
  }
\end{lstlisting}
\caption{A simple use of \lstinline{std::lock_guard} with a \lstinline{mutex}}
\label{lock-guard-ex}
\end{figure}


The \lstinline{lock_guard} class is the basic RAII class of the C++ library, a container for a single lock. \lstinline{lock_guard} is a templated class that takes an arbitrary \lstinline{BasicLockable} class as an argument, acquires it when constructed, and releases it when destroyed. A simple example of its use is shown in Figure~\ref{lock-guard-ex}; the mutex \lstinline{mutex_} is meant to protect the value of \lstinline{size}, and the \lstinline{lock_guard} object \lstinline{lock} in \lstinline{get_size} takes the place of calls to \lstinline{lock} and \lstinline{unlock}; \lstinline{mutex_} is \lstinline{lock}ed at line 5 and \lstinline{unlock}ed after reading \lstinline{size} but before \lstinline{get_size} returns.

Since \lstinline{lock_guard} is parameterized by a \lstinline{BasicLockable} class, our specification is likewise parameterized by a \lstinline{BasicLockable} instance. %not done yet
Constructing a \lstinline{lock_guard} with argument $m$ acquires $m$, and destroying it releases $m$: %adopt_lock?
%specs go here once we've made them generic

\subsection{\lstinline{scoped_lock}}

The \lstinline{scoped_lock} class takes a collection of locks as arguments, and acquires/releases them in an arbitrary fixed order, thus avoiding deadlock. %note this is also what std::lock does given multiple arguments

%specs go here once we've made them generic

\subsection{\lstinline{unique_lock}}
The \lstinline{unique_lock} class offers a more sophisticated RAII interface: the lock can be manually acquired and released through the \lstinline{unique_lock} as well as at construction/destruction, and the \lstinline{unique_lock} can be detached from one lock and attached to another during its lifetime. A \lstinline{unique_lock} object tracks whether it has acquired its associated mutex (if any), counting the acquisition from the constructor as well as explicit \lstinline{lock}/\lstinline{unlock} calls, and its destructor releases the mutex only if it is not currently acquired. %None of these operations are very complicated, but their specifications do need to account for many variations (no associated lock, associated lock is locked, associated lock is unlocked). %example?

The abstract state of a \lstinline{unique_lock} is of type $\mathsf{option}\ M$, which is $\mathsf{Some}\ m$ if a mutex $m$ is associated with the \lstinline{unique_lock} and $\mathsf{None}$ if no mutex is associated with it. %do we want to talk about move constructors/operators here?

%how much of this detail is useful? There are a lot of variations.
\[\begin{array}{c}
\{p \mapsto R(q, m) \ast \dolock{p}{m}{K}\}\\ \texttt{unique\_lock(p)}\\ \{u.\ u \mapsto \ulock(\mathsf{Some}\ (\mathsf{false}, p, q, m))\} \vspace{1em}\\%constructor notation?
\{u \mapsto \ulock(m)\ast \neg \mathsf{held}(m) \ast \dolock{\mathsf{ptr}(m)}{\mathsf{m}(m)}{K}\}\\ {\texttt{u.lock()}} \\ \{m \mapsto \ulock(m[\mathsf{held} := \mathsf{true}]) \ast K\}  \vspace{1em}\\
    \{u \mapsto \ulock(m)\ast \mathsf{held}(m) \ast \dounlock{\mathsf{ptr}(m)}{\mathsf{m}(m)}{K}\}\\ {\texttt{u.unlock}()}\\
    \{m \mapsto \ulock(m[\mathsf{held} := \mathsf{false}]) \ast K\}  \vspace{1em} \\
\{u \mapsto \ulock() \ast (\text{if } \mathsf{held}(m) \text{ then } \dounlock{\mathsf{ptr}(m)}{\mathsf{m}(m)}{K}\} \text{ else } K)\}\\ \texttt{u.}\!\!\sim\!\texttt{unique\_lock}()\\ \{K \ast \text{if } m \text{ then } \mathsf{ptr}(m) \mapsto R(\mathsf{q}(m), \mathsf{m}(m)) \text { else } \mathsf{emp}\} %destructor notation, Some/None notation
\end{array}\]
%verify the code from cppreference or a similar example?

\begin{figure}[htb]
\begin{lstlisting}
  int value{0};
  std::recursive_mutex m;

  void inc() {
    std::unique_lock<std::recursive_mutex> lk(m);
    value++;
  }

  void answer() {
    std::unique_lock<std::recursive_mutex> lk(m);
    value = 41;
    inc();
  }
\end{lstlisting}
\caption{A program with multiple \lstinline{unique_lock}s around a single \lstinline{recursive_mutex}}
\label{unique-recursive}
\end{figure}
As discussed in Section~\ref{basic-lockable}, the \lstinline{BasicLockable} requirement does not explicitly require that \lstinline{lock} lead to mutual exclusion, and indeed recursive mutexes can be \lstinline{lock}ed multiple times without being \lstinline{unlock}ed. This interacts in an interesting and useful way with \lstinline{unique_lock}'s acquisition tracking (the $\mathsf{held}$ predicate in our specifications): each \lstinline{unique_lock} can only acquire its mutex at most once, but we can construct multiple \lstinline{unique_lock}s around a single recursive mutex, each of which manages a single acquisition. %Is this equally true of lock_guard? We could call unlock once manually to illustrate the point.
The code in Figure~\ref{unique-recursive} shows how this can be used. When \lstinline{answer} is called, it acquires the recursive mutex \lstinline{m} by constructing a \lstinline{unique_lock} around it; it then calls \lstinline{inc}, which constructs another \lstinline{unique_lock} that acquires \lstinline{m} a second time. When each method returns, its \lstinline{unique_lock} is destroyed and \lstinline{m} is released once, so that \lstinline{m} is no longer locked after \lstinline{answer} returns. Our specifications can be used to verify this program. %proof outline?

\section{Case Study: Mutex Encapsulation}
%\input{ring_buffer.tex}
%TODO: find or make some interesting examples

We have seen that enforcing the requirements of C++ mutexes requires the management of thread-specific permission predicates that must be transferred between threads and locks. We have demonstrated that this is possible in simple examples of each mutex type; we now consider whether our approach is modular enough to scale to larger programs. In Section~\ref{mutex}, we explained that each mutex is given a user-chosen identifier $N$ when it is created (as opposed to, e.g., existentially quantifying the identifier in the postcondition of the constructor). In this section, we show how this approach lets us 1) demonstrate that two separate mutexes are indeed distinct, allowing a thread to acquire both of them at once, and 2) ensure that an arbitrary thread does not already hold an object's internal mutex, allowing the object's methods to register and unregister the thread when needed. The latter means that clients of an object with an internal mutex do not need to hold the thread-specific $\mathsf{not\_locked}$ predicate, so that ownership of the object can be transferred between threads, as is conventional in concurrent separation logic (but would be complicated by thread-specific predicates).
%There are at least two possible pitfalls. First, it might be difficult for a thread to acquire two different mutexes, because we need to manually prove that the second mutex is not the same as the first. Second and more subtly, thread-specific predicates might leak through layers of abstraction. Our mutex specifications must include predicates like $\notlocked{\gamma}{t}$ that explicitly mention thread IDs, but a data structure that uses a mutex internally should not need to expose thread IDs in its interface; it should be possible to share the data structure among threads exactly as one would a non-mutex-based implementation, without extra registration steps. In this section, we verify a case study showing that we avoid both these pitfalls, suggesting that our mutex specifications can indeed be used for modular verification.

\begin{figure}[htb]
\begin{lstlisting}
class Account {
private:
  unsigned long balance;
  std::recursive_mutex mut; // protects balance

public:
  explicit Account(unsigned long initial_balance) : balance(initial_balance) {}

  void incr_balance(unsigned long i) {
    std::lock_guard<std::recursive_mutex> lg(mut);
    balance += i;
  }

  void transfer_to(Account target, unsigned long i) {
    std::lock_guard<std::recursive_mutex> lg(mut);
    balance -= i;
    target.incr_balance(i);
  }
}

int main() {
  Account from{4};
  Account to{2};
  from.transfer_to(to, 3);
}
\end{lstlisting}
\caption{The code of our case study}
\label{transfer}
\end{figure}


The code of our case study is shown in Figure~\ref{transfer}. Each object of class \lstinline{Account} has a \lstinline{balance} protected by a mutex (in this code we use a \lstinline{recursive_mutex}, but any form of mutex would work). %make generic?
The \lstinline{transfer_to} method decrements the receiver's %terminology?
balance and increments the target object's balance, acquiring both mutexes in the process. Our questions are then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item How do we prove that we can acquire \lstinline{target}'s mutex, given that we already hold the receiver's mutex?
\item Can we use a representation predicate for \lstinline{Account} that does not include any thread-specific predicates and thus is freely transferable between threads?
\end{enumerate}

For question 2, recall that our specifications for \lstinline{recursive_mutex} are:
\[\begin{array}{c}
\{\currentthread{t} \ast m \mapsto_\pi \rmutex{N, \gamma}{P}\ast\acquirable{\gamma}{t}{n}{q}{P}{a}\}\\ {\texttt{m.lock()}} \\ \{\currentthread{t} \ast m \mapsto_\pi \rmutex{N, \gamma}{P}\ast \exists a'.\ \mathsf{acquire}(n, a, a') \ast \acquirable{N}{t}{n+1}{q}{P}{a'}\}  \vspace{1em}\\
    \{\currentthread{t} \ast m \mapsto_\pi \rmutex{N, \gamma}{P}\ast\acquirable{\gamma}{t}{n+1}{q}{P}{a}\}\\ {\texttt{m.unlock}()}\\
    \{\currentthread{t} \ast m \mapsto_\pi \rmutex{N, \gamma}{P}\ast\acquirable{\gamma}{t}{n}{q}{P}{a}\}
\end{array}\]
The $\mathsf{holds}$ predicate takes a thread $t$ that must match the current thread, and we must have it at line 15 %confirm
in order to acquire \lstinline{mut}. On the other hand, \lstinline{transfer_to} is a function that can be called by any thread that has access to the two accounts involved, and should have a specification like
\[ \{ a \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_A \ast b \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_B \}\ \texttt{a.transfer\_to(b, n)}\ \{ a \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_A \ast b \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_B \}\]
In particular, if $\mathsf{account}$ takes a thread $t$ as an argument, then we will not be able to freely transfer ownership of it between threads (since it would only be usable by that thread $t$). The mutex permission library allows us to isolate this thread-local information. 

The representation predicate for \lstinline{Account} is defined as
\[p \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_N \triangleq \exists \gamma.\ p.\texttt{mut} \mapsto_q \rmutex{N, \gamma}{\lambda n.\ p.\texttt{balance} \mapsto n} \ast \mathsf{token}_\gamma(q) %can we get away with this quantification?
\]
Ownership of an \lstinline{Account} is simply ownership of the mutex protecting the \lstinline{balance} field, plus ownership of the $\mathsf{token}$ that tracks whether the lock is held. In particular, it makes no mention of the $\mathsf{holds}$ predicate that appears in the precondition of the \lstinline{recursive_mutex} specifications (and explicitly takes a thread $t$ as an argument). When we create an account, we choose a namespace $N$ for that account, which in turn will be used as the namespace of its internal mutex field \lstinline{mut}. Inside member methods like \lstinline{incr_balance} and \lstinline{transfer_to} that acquire \lstinline{mut}, we register the calling thread with $N$, %recap the registration rule
acquire \lstinline{mut}, release \lstinline{mut} at the end of the method, and then unregister the thread. Registration requires both $\mutexperm{}{N}$ and $\token{N, \gamma}{q}$; the latter is part of $\mathsf{account}$, while the former is passed separately. Concretely, the specification we use for \lstinline{incr_balance} is:
\[\begin{array}{c}
\{ a \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_A \ast \mutexperm{t}{A} \ast \currentthread{t} \} \\ \texttt{a.incr\_balance(i)}\\ 
\{ a \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_A \ast \mutexperm{t}{A} \ast \currentthread{t} \} \end{array}\]
and the specification for \lstinline{transfer_to} is:
\[\begin{array}{c}\{ a \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_A \ast b \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_B \ast \mutexperm{t}{A} \ast \mutexperm{t}{B} \ast \currentthread{t} \}\\ \texttt{a.transfer\_to(b, n)}\\ \{ a \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_A \ast b \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_B  \ast \mutexperm{t}{A} \ast \mutexperm{t}{B} \ast \currentthread{t} \}
\end{array}\]
By choosing distinct namespaces $A \neq B$ for the two accounts (and thus their mutexes), we can easily obtain $\mutexperm{t}{A} \ast \mutexperm{t}{B}$ from a thread's starting $\mutexperm{t}{\top}$. The full proof outline for the example is shown in Figure~\ref{transfer-proof}.

\begin{figure}[htb]
\begin{lstlisting}[escapeinside    = {(*@}{@*)}]
class Account {
private:
  unsigned long balance;
  std::recursive_mutex mut; // protects balance

public:
  (*@ $\{ \mathsf{emp} \}$ @*)
  explicit Account(unsigned long initial_balance) : balance(initial_balance) {}
  (*@ $\{ a.\ a \mapsto \mathsf{account}_N \}$ @*)

  (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t} \ast a \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_A \ast \mutexperm{t}{A}  \}$ @*)
  void incr_balance(unsigned long i) {
    (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t} \ast a.\texttt{mut} \mapsto_q \rmutex{A, \gamma}{\lambda n.\,p.\texttt{balance} \mapsto n} \ast \mathsf{token}_\gamma(q) \ast \mutexperm{t}{A} \} \Rightarrow$ @*) 
    (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t} \ast a.\texttt{mut} \mapsto_q \rmutex{A, \gamma}{\lambda n.\,p.\texttt{balance} \mapsto n} \ast \notlocked{N, \gamma}{t}{q} \}$ @*) 
    std::lock_guard<std::recursive_mutex> lg(mut);
    balance += i;
    (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t} \ast a.\texttt{mut} \mapsto_q \rmutex{A, \gamma}{\lambda n.\ p.\texttt{balance} \mapsto n} \ast \notlocked{A, \gamma}{t}{q} \} \Rightarrow$ @*)
    (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t} \ast a.\texttt{mut} \mapsto_q \rmutex{A, \gamma}{\lambda n.\ p.\texttt{balance} \mapsto n} \ast \mathsf{token}_A(q) \ast \mutexperm{t}{A} \}$ @*)
  }
  (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t} \ast a \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_A \ast \mutexperm{t}{A}\}$ @*)

  void transfer_to(Account target, unsigned long i) { %%needs outline
    std::lock_guard<std::recursive_mutex> lg(mut);
    balance -= i;
    target.incr_balance(i);
  }
}

int main() {
  (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t_0} \ast \mutexperm{t_0}{\top} \}$ @*)
  Account from{4};
  Account to{2};
  (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t_0} \ast \mutexperm{t_0}{\top} \ast a \mapsto \mathsf{account}_A \ast b \mapsto \mathsf{account}_B \} \Rightarrow$ @*)
  (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t_0} \ast \mutexperm{t_0}{\top \setminus A \setminus B} \ast \mutexperm{t_0}{A} \ast \mutexperm{t_0}{B} \ast a \mapsto \mathsf{account}_A \ast b \mapsto \mathsf{account}_B \}$ @*)
  from.transfer_to(to, 3);
}
\end{lstlisting}
\caption{The proof outline of our case study}
\label{transfer-proof}
\end{figure}

Objects that make more complex use of locks may have to expose locked states (and thus thread-specific predicates) their clients, but at least in the case of objects that make balanced use of locks and always return to the client in an unlocked state, the thread-specific predicates can be handled internally and do not affect the representation predicate: instead, each thread separately manages its set of namespaces, and any thread that is not using the object's namespace for something else may call its methods. In this instance, the predicate $a \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_A$ could be transferred to any other thread, and that thread could call $a$'s methods as long as it is not currently holding a mutex with the namespace $A$. Because namespaces are chosen arbitrarily during verification, we can always choose different names for different objects, so that in practice any thread can use $a$. %make this more precise

\section{BRiCk Formalization}
Our specifications and examples are implemented in BRiCk, an Iris-based separation logic for C++. In this section we discuss some features of the implementation.

Although we use BRiCk to apply our specifications to C++ code, we expect that our formalisms can be reproduced in any Iris-based concurrent separation logic, whether theoretical (e.g., HeapLang) or realistic (e.g., RustBelt). The only nonstandard logical requirement is thread-specific predicates, but as discussed in Section~\ref{brick}, these can be implemented with a monotonic-predicate layer over an existing logic. Object-oriented languages are the most direct application, particularly for recursive mutexes, but non-OO languages such as C also have standard-library mutex implementations with the same thread restrictions (so our work could be usefully adapted to VST~\cite{vst}, for instance).

\section{Conclusion and Future Work}
While locks are widely used in concurrent separation logic, in many concurrent programming languages the standard CSL lock specs only accurately describe the behavior of inefficient implementations (e.g., spinlocks). More idiomatic and efficient mutex implementations such as Pthread make use of OS primitives that record and place restrictions on the threads accessing the mutex. We have demonstrated that these restrictions can be captured in separation logic specifications, through the combination of a fractional token and a system of per-thread mutex tracking, and that these features can be implemented with standard Iris ghost state plus a simple thread-specific predicate. This lets us give accurate specifications for basic, recursive, and shared mutexes from the C++ standard library, as well as the RAII classes that wrap these mutexes. Our specifications require additional mutex-tracking reasoning that is not needed when using naive lock specifications, but this reasoning is relatively simple to discharge and can be encapsulated, so that the client of an object with an internal mutex needs only reserve the object's namespace and does not need to directly reason about mutexes or thread-specific predicates.

C++'s thread support library includes many other concurrency primitives, such as condition variables (which allow more efficient mutex management), futures (which encapsulate asynchronous computations), and, as of the recent C++26 revision, RCU wrappers (for efficient concurrent memory reclamation). We are interested in extending our work to faithful specifications of these more sophisticated concurrency primitives. We are also interested in proving that our specifications are met by real standard-library mutex implementations (e.g., the Pthread mutex), which will require formalizing the interface provided by OS primitives such as \lstinline{futex}. %more
Ultimately, through careful attention to the informal specifications and existing implementations of standard libraries, we aim to bring the theory of concurrent separation logic to bear on concurrent programs as they are actually written.
